title: What lurks upstairs at the Amber Rose? A paranormal dinner investigates
excerpt: I sat in the upstairs banquet hall of the Amber Rose Restaurant in Old North Dayton, at a table with two skeptics and two content creators. In between us were fried sauerkraut balls, pierogies, pretzels, beer cheese and an EMF reader for every chair.
content:
I sat in the upstairs banquet hall of the Amber Rose Restaurant in Old North Dayton, at a table with two skeptics and two content creators. In between us were fried sauerkraut balls, pierogies, pretzels, beer cheese and an EMF reader for every chair.

The Amber Rose is reputedly haunted. Built around 1910 by Sigmund Ksiezopolski, the building originally housed Sig’s General Store and Deli, a gathering place for the Polish community. Ksiezopolski’s family lived upstairs, where many of us are now eating cabbage rolls.

We were there for the Haunted Supper Series, an event by Ohio-based paranormal company Eerie Excursions. Founders Beth Fontaine and Kayla Simonton combine dinner at historic restaurants with guided paranormal investigations.

“I was always told the upstairs was the thing,” I said to Beth and Kayla, referring to the rumored spiritual activity involving a woman in a ruffled dress who appears at the windows.

“It’s all of it,” Beth said.

When asked what the most active area was, Beth mentioned the bathrooms, one of which could be accessed in the room we were standing in. The lid of the trash can allegedly wanders off on its own from time to time.

The two have more than 15 years of hands-on investigative experience. Beth and her husband ran Para Adventures, a haunted tourism company. Kayla would investigate on her own. They started Eerie Excursions three years ago.

“I had so many things happen when I was a kid, and I thought everybody had it because it was so normal to me,” Beth said. “I was like, Oh, you don’t have a man walking across your living room?”

Beth recalled walking through Crawford Woods in Hamilton as a child with two friends. A boy appeared. He was a full-bodied figure, but he looked different, possibly sepia-toned. They asked if he was real, then he disappeared.

One of Kayla’s earlier experiences was in Gettysburg, where she saw three soldiers walking across a battlefield.

“The more you do this and talk to everyone, everyone has a ghost story,” Kayla said. “History is a huge part of this for us, too. We love preservation.”

Beth and Kayla aren’t easily frightened, though each has their limits. For Beth, it’s things crawling on the floors and walls. For Kayla, it’s bats and living people. I can confirm this, as she jumped when I once talked over her shoulder. I apologized for spooking her. She replied: “You know what we do, right?”

One of the skeptics at my table, Aaron, once had plans to become a priest. Paranormal radio show host Art Bell and the Christopher Walken movie “Communion” convinced him to veer from the cloth life. Aaron bought tickets for the haunted supper event for his wife Kelly for both her birthday and their anniversary. His skepticism would be tested as the night progressed.

The Amber Rose was my third paranormal investigation, after visits to the Spaghetti Warehouse and Poasttown Elementary. I’ve settled into cautious skepticism: I’m open to the idea of spirits, but I’d rather they not bother me.

This, Kayla said, will either make it happen or keep them away.

After dinner, Beth and Kayla shared more of the building’s history. The restaurant is said to be haunted by Genevieve “Chickie” Ksiezopolski, Sig’s daughter, who lived in the building. She is also believed to be the woman sometimes reported in the upstairs windows.

“If something scares you tonight,” Beth said, “do not run.”

Kayla passed around photographs of the general store and its original residents. Then the lights went out, and everyone switched on their EMF detectors. The devices register changes in electromagnetic fields, but those readings alone can’t establish paranormal activity. Even a text can set them off. Glow sticks were wrapped around wrists or worn like necklaces for anyone venturing outside the guided tour.

Onto and around the bartop, Beth and Kayla laid out a REM-POD, the Flux, LED cat balls, a music box and a Maglite flashlight, communication tools between us and them. Various EMF detectors jumped from green to orange to red, the results glowing on the ceiling.

Kayla then introduced Patrick, a doll wearing a sailor’s uniform. He has two bells on his hands and a motion sensor that triggers when he’s moved. Speaking for the room, he was the scariest thing we’d all witnessed thus far into the night.

The two then activated the Phasmabox, a program they use in an attempt to communicate with spirits. Guests called out questions from around the room: Are you stuck here? Are you free to come and go? Is it safe here tonight? Would you like a drink?

The Flux and antenna devices went off in quick succession. Voices came through the Phasmabox (especially after that last question) but were mostly unintelligible sounds that sometimes seemed to resemble familiar words. Perhaps the spirits were speaking Polish.

Barry and Cookie Burke, an older couple who had investigated several locations with Eerie Excursions, brought their own equipment. Barry used an SLS camera, which processes depth-sensor data to display stick figures over shapes its software interprets as humanlike.

I asked Barry if he’s ever concerned about paranormal activity. He said he approaches investigations with a firm boundary: He doesn’t believe spirits can hurt him or follow him home. He’s there to learn.

Lights flickered and speech was detected via the Phasmabox and smartphone apps. We descended the stairs to the basement.

Beth and Kayla described the basement as a former gathering place associated with alleged gambling, womanizing and bowling. The remnants of the bowling alley, Studio B, are painted on the cement walls of one of the rooms.

The trigger light inside Patrick rapidly turned on and off. EMF detectors fluctuated around orange and red. There are unverified claims of a child dying here. Some guests interpreted the doll’s movements as a sign that a child spirit was interacting with it. Barry’s SLS camera displayed a jumbled stick figure that appeared to crawl across the floor, which Beth did not appreciate all that much.

Kayla silenced the room to record potential EVPs, or an electronic voice phenomenon. A simple digital recorder can capture faint sounds, but cannot necessarily establish that they are paranormal voices, especially in a larger group.

“At this point, this is when your stomach’s gonna growl insanely loud,” Kayla said. As if on cue, the pierogies and sauerkraut started their digestion. “Right off the bat, Brandon. So proud of you.”

There was a tightness in my chest that I hadn’t felt upstairs, the hair-raising sensation of needing to quickly run up some stairs. I saw someone or something to my left move. Acknowledgment makes it real. I remained still and in the dark. I did not run.

“Is anyone feeling extremely brave tonight?” Kayla asked. Aaron, our skeptic, volunteered as tribute.

Fitted with headphones and a cheap AM/FM radio, Aaron listened to white noise to see if anything from the other side came through. If anything touched him, he was to report that out loud.

“Back there is the abyss,” Kayla said, referring to the bleak darkness in the distance.

“I see that,” I told her.

Aaron stood in the old musty bowling alley, lightly mouthing questions to whoever may want to answer. He clutched his chest at one point, then moved to the other side of the room.

“All of us have psychic ability,” Kayla said. “So when you’re listening to static, you’re using your inner self to pick up and hear voices. You’re really out of everything. It’s kind of like sensory deprivation.”

I told her that Aaron was skeptical. She perceived him to be sensitive.

“At one point, I felt very cold and very hot,” Aaron said, removing the headphones. “That’s why I moved. Then I felt it again.”

It was not long after that Aaron and Kelly left. He shook my hand before ascending the steps. His eyes appeared vaguely different than when I met him in the banquet hall.

Eventually, Z-93 Morning Z host Scott Sharp and I ventured into the upstairs bathroom. I’d neglected to tell him that earlier in the night, I’d seen what looked like a transparent head poking out from inside it.

As we crossed the threshold, we both felt as though we’d walked through something unexplainable. I left Scott alone with the dousing rods. The paper towel dispenser went off on its own — a moment Scott audibly did not appreciate — but the trash can lid remained intact.

Around 1 a.m., we exited the building, thanking the spirits for their time and asking them not to follow us home.

We’d embraced the eerie. The eerie knew that we’d be back again.

Brandon Berry covers the music and arts scene in Dayton and southwest Ohio. Reach him at branberry100@gmail.com.
